Key_Findings: Heptane droplets exhibited two-stage combustion: after the visible hot flame extinguished, a low-temperature 'cool flame' continued burning invisibly, consuming fuel and producing formaldehyde and carbon monoxide.
AI_Summary: Liquid fuels in space can keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' even after a fire looks completely out, silently generating toxic gases.
Safety_Recommendations: Install multi-spectrum UV/IR and gas-phase CO/formaldehyde sensors rather than relying solely on visible-light smoke detectors.

Key_Findings: Large-scale 1-meter cotton-fiberglass sample burned rapidly in low-speed forced airflow, demonstrating that standard 1-g NASA-STD-6001 upward flame tests underestimate microgravity flame spread rates.
AI_Summary: Large fabric and composite surfaces burn faster in gentle spacecraft ventilation currents than ground tests predict.
Safety_Recommendations: Restrict exposed large-area textiles in high-airflow corridors and enforce automated ventilation shutoff upon smoke detection.

Key_Findings: Elevated oxygen levels (26.5% exploration atmosphere) significantly increased ignition propensity and toxic CO/HCN output during smoldering combustion.
AI_Summary: Future Moon and Mars habitats using higher oxygen levels face severe toxic gas hazards from smoldering plastics and fabrics.
Safety_Recommendations: Enforce strict material off-gassing limits and equip exploration cabins with rapid scrubbing systems for carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide.

Key_Findings: Low-speed ventilation airflow (5-15 cm/s) enhances oxygen delivery to the flame front in microgravity, allowing thin solids to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.
AI_Summary: Gentle air circulation inside spacecraft actually feeds small solid fires, allowing them to survive in lower oxygen levels.
Safety_Recommendations: Design cabin ventilation zones with emergency isolation dampers to immediately cut airflow to any compartment with a fire alarm.

Key_Findings: Spherical diffusion flames in microgravity showed lower soot radiation losses, enabling stable combustion near extinction limits with minimal visible luminosity.
AI_Summary: Gas leaks in microgravity can sustain nearly invisible flames at very low oxygen concentrations without rising heat plumes.
Safety_Recommendations: Use ultrasonic leak detectors and distributed catalytic gas sensors around all propulsion and life-support propellant lines.

Key_Findings: Partial gravity (0.16g) creates weak buoyant plumes that draw fresh oxygen into the flame base, producing faster flame spread than pure microgravity for thick polymers.
AI_Summary: Fires on a Lunar base (1/6th Earth gravity) spread faster across thick plastics than they do aboard the International Space Station.
Safety_Recommendations: Upgrade Lunar habitat fire suppression nozzles and select flame-retardant fluoropolymers for all structural interior panels.

Key_Findings: Radiative heat feedback from nearby walls in narrow spacecraft racks accelerates flame spread and traps dense soot in all directions.
AI_Summary: Fires inside tight equipment racks heat surrounding walls and spread much faster than fires in open cabin areas.
Safety_Recommendations: Line avionics bays with non-combustible aerogel insulation and place aspirated smoke detectors directly inside rack exhaust ducts.

Experiment_Name: BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids II)
Key_Findings: Thick solid fuels require sustained external heat flux to maintain pyrolysis in microgravity and self-extinguish rapidly once ventilation airflow drops below 2 cm/s.
AI_Summary: Thick plastic components are hard to keep burning in space and usually go out on their own if cabin fans are turned off.
Safety_Recommendations: Use thick, high-density structural polymers where possible and link fan-power cutoffs directly to local thermal sensors.

Key_Findings: Extended cool-flame burning regimes were observed for heavy hydrocarbon surrogates, producing persistent aldehydes and peroxides without soot formation.
AI_Summary: Heavy liquid fuels can undergo prolonged flameless oxidation in space, creating corrosive and toxic vapors without producing smoke.
Safety_Recommendations: Pair optical smoke alarms with chemical vapor sensors in payload racks handling liquid coolants or hydrocarbon fluids.

Key_Findings: Electrical wire insulation tested under simulated Martian gravity showed molten polymer dripping and sustained flame propagation along copper conductors.
AI_Summary: Overheated electrical wires in Martian habitats can drip burning plastic and carry fire along cable bundles.
Safety_Recommendations: Mandate PTFE/Kapton aerospace-grade wire insulation and install arc-fault circuit interrupters on all habitat power buses.

Key_Findings: A 100% pure oxygen environment at 16.7 psi turned Velcro, nylon, and foam padding into explosive fuels, causing fatal cabin flashover within 17 seconds.
AI_Summary: Pure oxygen cabin atmospheres make ordinary materials explosively flammable, leaving virtually zero time for crew escape.
Safety_Recommendations: Never use pure 100% oxygen atmospheres in crewed cabins; maintain nitrogen-diluted mixed-gas atmospheres and outward-opening quick-release hatches.

Key_Findings: A solid-fuel perchlorate oxygen candle spontaneously ignited during routine activation, burning for 14 minutes and filling the station with acrid smoke and toxic particulates, blocking one of two Soyuz escape routes.
AI_Summary: A routine oxygen candle turned into a 14-minute inferno that filled Mir with toxic smoke and blocked the emergency exit — revealing that chemical O2 generators are a severe fire hazard.
Safety_Recommendations: Replace chemical oxygen generators with electrolytic systems; keep at least two clear egress paths at all times; store emergency SCBA masks within 3 seconds reach of every crew station.

Key_Findings: A damaged Teflon-insulated wire inside oxygen tank 2 caused an electrical arc, igniting the insulation and rupturing the tank; the resulting explosion crippled the Service Module and forced use of the Lunar Module as a lifeboat.
AI_Summary: A manufacturing defect turned a routine stir command into a catastrophic explosion that cut power and oxygen mid-mission — crew survived only by improvising a lunar module lifeboat.
Safety_Recommendations: Implement triple-redundant oxygen storage; conduct rigorous pre-flight wiring inspections; design every crewed spacecraft with an independent safe-haven module capable of sustaining crew for 96+ hours.

Key_Findings: Confirmed cool-flame phenomenon across a wider droplet size range; CO2 suppression agents were less effective than on Earth due to altered gas-phase transport in microgravity.
AI_Summary: Even the most common fire extinguisher gas (CO2) works less effectively in space — fires may need longer suppression bursts to fully extinguish.
Safety_Recommendations: Increase CO2 extinguisher discharge time by at least 40% over Earth recommendations and verify chemical extinction with onboard gas analyzers before declaring fire out.

Key_Findings: Nine different spacecraft materials tested; cotton-fiberglass composite showed highest spread rate while silicone-coated Nomex self-extinguished consistently — validating NASA-approved material selections.
AI_Summary: Not all spacecraft-approved fabrics behave equally in space fires — some self-extinguish while others spread flames rapidly even in the same environment.
Safety_Recommendations: Preference silicone-coated Nomex and flame-barrier laminates over cotton composites for all crew-worn garments and soft goods in habitat interiors.

Key_Findings: Increasing forced airflow velocity from 10 to 20 cm/s doubled the flame spread rate, confirming that spacecraft ventilation systems are a primary driver of fire growth in microgravity.
AI_Summary: Doubling cabin ventilation speed doubles how fast a fire spreads — the life-support fans keeping crew alive can rapidly escalate a fire emergency.
Safety_Recommendations: Integrate two-speed emergency fan mode: normal ops at 10 cm/s, automatic reduction to 2 cm/s on first smoke alarm to starve fire without cutting crew oxygen supply.

Key_Findings: Thin PMMA sheets self-extinguished in quiescent microgravity below 20% oxygen; flame spread rate was strongly dependent on sample width and airflow velocity rather than gravity.
AI_Summary: Thin plastic sheets often go out on their own in the still air of a spacecraft — but only if no ventilation is blowing across them.
Safety_Recommendations: Store thin-film plastics (packaging, labels, bags) in sealed containers away from ventilation ducts; treat any loose film near a vent as a potential fire fuel source.
